sections.h2: Where do you record a deed in Yavapai County?
sections.html:
You record a deed with the Yavapai County Recorder, which keeps two counters. The Prescott office is at 1015 Fair Street, Room 228, Prescott, AZ 86305. The Cottonwood office is at 10 S 6th Street, Cottonwood, AZ 86326.

The county's recorder fee schedule gives (928) 771-3244, option 6, for Prescott and (928) 639-5807 for Cottonwood. Questions can also go to web.recorder@yavapaiaz.gov. Prescott is the county seat, and Cottonwood is the second counter.

The Recorder's page says the office records real estate transactions, mortgages, deeds of trust, family trusts, and subdivision plats and surveys. For a house sale, the document you care about is the deed, plus any release of the old mortgage or deed of trust that your title company records at the same time.

sections.h2: What does the Yavapai County Recorder charge?
sections.html:
The county fee schedule, updated April 28, 2025, lists a flat $30.00 for all instruments. That amount covers the affidavit of property value, extra indexing, the state surcharge and return postage, so a typical deed does not pick up a stack of add-on charges.

ItemAmount on the county schedule
All instruments, including the affidavit of property value$30.00
Government agencies, paid from public funds$15.00
Maps, plats and land surveys, first page / each added page$24.00 / $20.00
Copy of a deed or similar record, per page$1.00
Certification, each document$3.00
Military discharge recordsFree

Source: Yavapai County Recorder fee schedule (cites A.R.S. 11-475 for the recording fee increase). The schedule shows no separate transfer-tax line. Call the Recorder before you send a check, since the county revises the sheet from time to time.

sections.h2: What has to be attached to a deed before it is accepted?
sections.html:
Most deeds need an affidavit of legal value. Under A.R.S. 11-1133, a deed that transfers title must carry an affidavit signed by the seller and buyer, or their agents, on a form approved by the Department of Revenue. The recorder must refuse to record a deed if the affidavit is incomplete, unless the deed carries a notation for an exemption.

The statute lists what the affidavit has to state:

  • names, mailing addresses and phone numbers of buyer and seller, and where the tax statement should go
  • the full legal description, the situs address and the assessor's parcel number
  • the date of sale, the total price, the cash down payment and the type of financing
  • whether personal property worth five percent or more of the price changed hands
  • how the home will be used, including whether it will be owner-occupied or rented

A.R.S. 11-1134 excuses certain transfers, among them a deed of gift, a conveyance made under a court order, a quitclaim executed for no money, and transfers of residential property for nominal consideration between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or siblings. Whoever claims an exemption must write the specific exemption on the face of the instrument.

sections.h2: Can you record or order copies without going to the counter?
sections.html:
Yes. The county's fee schedule lists several ways to deal with the Recorder, and only one of them requires a visit. Each path has its own rules, so pick the one that fits the timing of your closing.

  • Web recording. The Recorder's page announces an online portal run through Tyler Technologies (tylertech.com/webrecording). You register for an account and submit documents from home or an office.
  • In person. Walk the document into the Prescott or Cottonwood counter.
  • Self-service search. The schedule points to an online search of recorded documents on the county website.
  • Mail for copies. Send a written request or the county's official copy request form to Yavapai County Recorder, 1015 Fair St, Room 228, Prescott, AZ 86305. Include a self-addressed stamped envelope large enough for the order and make the check payable to Yavapai County Recorder.

The forms page also carries a copy request form, commercial and non-commercial record request forms, a Social Security number redaction form and a DD-214 military discharge request form.

sections.h2: What should a Yavapai County seller know about the county?
sections.html:
Yavapai County covers 8,128 square miles in central Arizona, with terrain that runs from the lower Sonoran Desert in the south up to the Coconino Plateau and the Mogollon Rim. Prescott is the seat. Its 2020 census population was 236,209.

The Treasurer's list of taxing jurisdictions names towns and cities including Prescott, Prescott Valley, Cottonwood, Camp Verde, Clarkdale, Jerome and Wickenburg, along with Ash Fork, Bagdad, Congress, Mayer and Seligman. School districts on the same list include Prescott Unified, Humboldt Unified, Chino Valley Unified, Camp Verde Unified, Sedona Unified and Mingus Union High School.

Prices have eased this year. In a November 2, 2026 release, Assessor Judd Simmons reported a median single-family sales price of $539,000 for sales recorded through October, down 2.9 percent from $555,000 in 2025. A recorded deed is what feeds that sales data, so an accurate affidavit helps keep the county's numbers clean.

sections.h2: How do recorded documents connect to your tax bill and liens?
sections.html:
Recording a deed does not wipe out a tax lien. Under A.R.S. 42-17153, the property tax lien attaches on January 1 of the tax year and stays until the taxes, penalties, charges and interest are paid. It ranks ahead of other liens and encumbrances, apart from liens held by the state and liens for taxes from other years.

That is why the title company asks the Yavapai County Treasurer for a payoff figure before closing. The Treasurer's FAQ says that if you sold before the bill arrived, the new owner or mortgage company pays the current-year bill, and that taxes due are the responsibility of the current owner. Tax bills for Yavapai County are mailed by the end of September. Under A.R.S. 42-18052, the first half is delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and the second half after 5:00 p.m. on May 1, so a closing between those dates should settle whichever installment is open.

The Recorder's FAQ also covers homestead protection, which it describes as automatic and limited. It points readers to A.R.S. 33-1101 through 33-1105 and tells them to ask an attorney about their own situation, since the office cannot give legal advice.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Yavapai County?
faqs.a: The county fee schedule updated April 28, 2025 lists $30.00 for all instruments, which includes the affidavit of property value, extra indexing, the state surcharge and return postage. Government agencies paying from public funds are listed at $15.00. Call the Recorder at (928) 771-3244, option 6, to confirm the amount before you mail a check.

faqs.q: Does Yavapai County charge a transfer tax on a home sale?
faqs.a: The county's recorder fee schedule shows one $30.00 instrument charge and no transfer-tax line. Ask the Recorder or your title company whether anything else applies to your deed. The affidavit of legal value under A.R.S. 11-1133 is required, and that cost is built into the $30.00.

faqs.q: Can I record a Yavapai County deed online?
faqs.a: Yes. The Recorder's page announces an online web-recording portal through Tyler Technologies, where you register for an account and submit documents. Title and escrow companies usually handle this step for a sale, but individual owners can also use it.

faqs.q: Which deeds do not need the affidavit of legal value?
faqs.a: Deeds listed in A.R.S. 11-1134, such as a deed of gift, a conveyance under a court order, a quitclaim for no money, and certain nominal-consideration transfers between close family members. The instrument must show the specific exemption on its face when it is recorded.

faqs.q: How do I get a certified copy of my Yavapai County deed?
faqs.a: Use the county's official copy request form or a written request, mail it to Yavapai County Recorder, 1015 Fair St, Room 228, Prescott, AZ 86305, and include a self-addressed stamped envelope. The fee schedule lists $1.00 per page for copies plus $3.00 for each certification. You can also ask at the Prescott or Cottonwood counter.
